verses.text: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, like some people, letters of recommendation to you or from you?
You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts, known and read by everyone.
It is clear that you are a letter from Christ, the result of our ministry, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
Such confidence before God is ours through Christ.
Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim that anything comes from us, but our competence comes from God.
And He has qualified us as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
Now if the ministry of death, which was engraved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at the face of Moses because of its fleeting glory,
will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious?
For if the ministry of condemnation was glorious, how much more glorious is the ministry of righteousness!
Indeed, what was once glorious has no glory now in comparison to the glory that surpasses it.
For if what was fading away came with glory, how much greater is the glory of that which endures!
Therefore, since we have such a hope, we are very bold.
We are not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away.
But their minds were closed. For to this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant. It has not been lifted, because only in Christ can it be removed.
And even to this day when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts.
But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.
Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
And we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.

context.author: Paul the apostle, with Timothy (1:1)
context.genre: Letter, personal and defensive, among Paul’s most emotional
context.audience: The church in Corinth, after a painful period of conflict
context.setting: Rival teachers had arrived in Corinth with letters of recommendation. Paul says the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit on hearts. He contrasts the ministry of the old covenant, written on stone, with the new covenant of the Spirit, and compares Moses’ veiled face with the unveiled face of believers.
context.custom: Letters of recommendation were a common way for traveling teachers to win trust. The veil on Moses’ face (Exodus 34:29-35) is read by Paul as a picture of how many Jews still read the old covenant without understanding that Christ fulfills it.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 4 continues, with the treasure of the gospel in fragile clay jars.
context.timelineBible: Paul draws on Exodus 34 (Moses’ shining face), Jeremiah 31:31-34 and Ezekiel 36:26-27 (the new covenant and the Spirit on hearts), and Exodus 24 (tablets of stone).
context.sparkNotes: The Corinthians are Paul’s letter of recommendation, written by the Spirit on human hearts. The old covenant killed, but the Spirit gives life. Moses’ glory faded, while the glory of the new covenant lasts. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom, and believers are being transformed into his image.

translation.meaning: The same verb that is used of Jesus’ transfiguration. Believers are slowly changed into the image of the Lord.
Release, as of a slave. The Spirit sets believers free from the old way of the written code.

otBackground.note: Moses’ face shone, and he veiled it.
A new heart and a new spirit.

overview.summary: Paul says the church is his living letter, and he is a minister of a new covenant of the Spirit. Believers behold the Lord’s glory with unveiled faces and are being transformed.
overview.settingLine: Paul writes from Macedonia to the church in Corinth.

history.t: They arrived with letters and credentials and questioned Paul.
Moses covered his face after speaking with God, and Paul says the glory was fading.

customs.t: A letter of introduction was a basic form of trust in the Roman world.
Jews read Moses in the synagogue, and Paul says a veil lies over their reading.

archaeology.t: Stone tablets from antiquity illustrate what “written on stone” meant.
A stone from Corinth bears the inscription “Synagogue of the Hebrews,” perhaps from a later period.

overview.discussion: Paul says we are being transformed from one degree of glory to another. In what area of my life do I sense that God is changing me?
overview.book: The second letter to the Corinthians · 13 chapters. Paul’s most personal letter, written to heal a strained relationship.
overview.author: Paul
